title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
directAnswer: Each bar is the height of some rectangle; the question is how far left and right that height can extend before it hits a shorter bar. Brute force checks every bar's reach by scanning outward, O(n²). The optimal answer keeps a monotonic increasing stack of bar indices: when a bar shorter than the stack top arrives, the top bar can't extend any further right, so you pop it and finalise its rectangle. Each bar is pushed and popped once — O(n).

remember.pattern: Monotonic increasing stack of indices; pop finalises a rectangle
remember.formula:
for i in 0..n:                # i == n acts as a height-0 sentinel
    h = (i < n) ? heights[i] : 0
    while stack not empty and heights[stack.top] >= h:
        height = heights[stack.pop()]
        width  = stack.empty() ? i : i - stack.top - 1
        best   = max(best, height * width)
    stack.push(i)
rules: Push **indices**, not heights — you need the index to compute width as `i - newTop - 1`.
When you pop bar `h`, its **right boundary** is the current index `i` and its **left boundary** is the new stack top after popping.
Width is `i - stack.top - 1` after popping; if the stack is empty, `h` extends all the way left, so width is `i`.
Append a virtual **0-height bar** at the end (or loop to `i == n`) to flush every remaining bar off the stack.
The stack stays **non-decreasing** in height — that invariant is why each popped bar's reach is exactly known.
whenToUse: Maximum-area / span problem where each element's value is a height and neighbours bound its reach
You need, for each element, the nearest strictly smaller element on the left and right
Histogram, skyline, or 'maximal rectangle' in a binary matrix (run this per row)
Any 'expand while neighbours are at least as tall' computation in one pass
antiSignals: You only need the single tallest bar → that's just a max, no stack
Bars can be negative / it's not an area problem → monotonic-stack framing doesn't apply
You need every rectangle, not the largest → enumeration, not this greedy pop
The array is tiny and clarity matters more than speed → brute force is fine
remember.takeaway: The monotonic stack answers 'how far can this height extend?' for every bar in one pass. The key realisation: a bar's rectangle is fixed exactly when a shorter bar appears on its right — that's the moment to pop and measure. This is the engine behind Maximal Rectangle, Trapping Rain Water, and Next Greater Element.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that each bar's maximal rectangle is bounded by the nearest shorter bar on each side, and whether you can compute both boundaries in a single monotonic-stack pass instead of two outward scans.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Storing heights instead of indices (so width can't be computed), or mishandling the width as i - top - 1 after popping, especially the empty-stack case where the bar reaches the far left.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the invariant: the stack holds bars in increasing height, so when you pop, the new top is exactly the nearest shorter bar on the left and the current index is the nearest shorter (or equal) bar on the right. Mention the sentinel that flushes the stack.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `heights` representing the heights of bars in a histogram, where each bar has width `1`. Find the area of the **largest rectangle** that can be formed within the bounds of the histogram.

The rectangle must be axis-aligned and made of consecutive bars; its height is limited by the **shortest** bar it spans.
constraints: Area can exceed 32-bit range → use 64-bit (long) for the running maximum
understanding: Fix a bar as the limiting (shortest) height of a rectangle. The rectangle then stretches left and right until it meets a bar strictly shorter than this one. So for every bar you want the nearest strictly smaller bar on each side; the width between those boundaries times the bar's height is that bar's best rectangle. The answer is the max over all bars.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can heights be zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A zero-height bar contributes no area but acts as a hard wall that no rectangle crosses — useful to reason about, and exactly why a virtual 0 at the end flushes the stack.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the area get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to ~10⁵ × 10⁹ = 10¹⁴, which overflows 32-bit. Use a 64-bit accumulator for the maximum area.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do ties (equal heights) matter for the boundary?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: You can treat the right boundary as the nearest bar that is strictly shorter, and pop on >= so equal bars merge correctly. Either consistent convention works as long as each rectangle is counted once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the rectangle required to use whole bars?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — bars have width 1 and the rectangle spans a contiguous run of them, capped by the shortest in that run.

examples.explanation: Bars 5 and 6 (indices 2,3) form height 5 over width 2 = 10. No taller-by-wider rectangle beats it.
Either the single bar of height 4 (area 4) or both bars at height 2 (area 4). Both give 4.
Bars at indices 2..4 (5,4,5) give height 4 over width 3 = 12.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Expand Each Bar Outward
approaches.whenToMention: State it to anchor the O(n²) baseline, then say the repeated outward scans are what the stack removes.
hints: Make each bar the limiting height. How wide can a rectangle of that exact height be? It stops the moment a shorter bar appears on either side.
For each index i, walk left while bars are >= heights[i], walk right while bars are >= heights[i]. The width is right - left + 1.
area = heights[i] × width. Take the max over all i. Two outward scans per bar is the O(n²) cost.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n bars you may scan up to n-1 bars to the left and right to find where the height can no longer extend. That's O(n) work per bar, O(n²) overall. No extra data structures, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Treat every bar as the shortest bar of some candidate rectangle. The rectangle's height is then fixed at `heights[i]`, and its width is however far that height can stretch in both directions before hitting a strictly shorter bar.

**Why fix the shortest bar.** Any rectangle has a single limiting height — its shortest bar. If you enumerate over 'which bar is the limiter', you cover every possible rectangle exactly once. So for bar `i`, expand left and right while neighbouring bars are at least `heights[i]`; the moment you hit something shorter, that side's wall is set.

**Computing the width.** Let `left` be the first index going left that is shorter than `heights[i]`, and `right` the first going right that is shorter. The rectangle spans `right - left - 1` bars, all at least `heights[i]` tall, so its area is `heights[i] × (right - left - 1)`.

**Why it's slow and where it repeats work.** A nearly-sorted-ascending histogram like `[1,2,3,...,n]` makes each bar scan all the way to one end, so the outward walks cost `O(n)` each and the total is quadratic. Crucially, those scans recompute the same boundaries over and over — the bar to your left already knew where the next shorter bar was. A stack lets you remember that instead of rescanning, which is the leap to the linear solution.
approaches.insight: Every rectangle is uniquely identified by its shortest bar, so iterating over 'which bar is the limiter' is complete. The inefficiency is rediscovering each bar's left/right shorter-neighbour from scratch — exactly the boundaries a monotonic stack computes once.

pitfalls: Multiplying int width by int height without casting to long — overflow on large inputs.
Using > instead of >= and double-counting or missing equal-height runs.
Believing the outward scans are cheap — they are O(n) each on a monotone histogram.

approaches.name: Monotonic Increasing Stack (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'keep indices of bars in increasing height; pop and measure when a shorter bar arrives'.
hints: When you're standing on bar i, which earlier bars still have an 'open' rectangle that could extend to i? Only those shorter than or equal to bar i — the taller ones were already cut off.

Keep a stack of indices whose heights are non-decreasing. When a new bar is shorter than the top, the top bar can't extend past i, so finalise it: pop, its right wall is i and its left wall is the new top.
Width after popping index t is i - stack.top - 1, or i if the stack is now empty. Append a virtual 0 at the end so every leftover bar gets popped and measured.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once. All other work per step is O(1). With at most n pushes and n pops over the whole run, the total is O(n) time. The stack holds at most n indices, so O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a stack of bar indices whose heights are non-decreasing from bottom to top. Walk left to right; at each new bar (and one final virtual bar of height 0), pop every stacked bar that is at least as tall as the current one, finalising its rectangle as you pop.

**The invariant and why it's everything.** The stack is always non-decreasing in height. So for any bar still on the stack, every bar below it is shorter — meaning the bar directly below is its **nearest shorter bar on the left**. When a new bar at index `i` is shorter than the top, that top bar has just met its **nearest shorter bar on the right**: index `i`. Both walls are now known in O(1), which is exactly what the brute force re-scanned for.

**Computing the width on pop.** Pop the top index `t` with height `heights[t]`. Its right wall is `i` (the bar that triggered the pop). Its left wall is whatever is now on top of the stack — the nearest shorter bar to the left — at index `newTop`. The rectangle spans the bars strictly between those walls: width `i - newTop - 1`. If the stack is empty after popping, no shorter bar exists to the left, so the bar reaches the far-left edge and width is just `i`.

**Why pop on `>=` and not only `>`.** Popping when the top is equal in height as well keeps the measurement clean: an equal bar's rectangle will be re-discovered from the surviving bar of the same height, so no area is lost, and you avoid leaving stale equal bars that complicate the width math. Either a strict or non-strict convention works as long as it's consistent; `>=` is the simplest to reason about.

**The sentinel that flushes the stack.** After the last real bar, bars that never met a shorter neighbour on the right are still on the stack. Processing one extra index `i = n` with height `0` (shorter than everything) forces every remaining bar to pop and be measured, with right wall `n`. That's why the loop runs to `i == n`.

**Why it's O(n).** Push happens once per index. A pop also happens at most once per index — once finalised, a bar never returns. So across the entire pass there are at most `n` pushes and `n` pops; the inner `while` is amortised O(1). Linear time, with the stack as the only extra memory.
approaches.insight: The stack turns 'find the nearest shorter bar on each side' — two outward scans in the brute force — into a single forward pass. The reusable idea: a monotonic stack remembers candidates whose answer isn't decided yet and resolves each the instant its boundary appears. The same engine solves Next Greater Element, Trapping Rain Water, and Maximal Rectangle (run this per matrix row).

code.python:
def largest_rectangle(heights: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(heights)
    stack: list[int] = []
    best = 0
    for i in range(n + 1):
        h = 0 if i == n else heights[i]
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1
            best = max(best, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(largest_rectangle([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]))

pitfalls: Pushing heights instead of indices — you lose the ability to compute width.
Forgetting the trailing sentinel, leaving the tallest bars unmeasured.
Getting the width wrong when the stack empties — it should be i, not i - 1.
Using int for the area accumulator and overflowing.

commonMistakes: Storing bar heights on the stack instead of indices, so width is uncomputable.
Forgetting the virtual 0-height bar at the end, leaving remaining bars unmeasured.
Computing area in 32-bit and overflowing on large histograms.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Pushing heights instead of indices
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Width depends on positions: i - newTop - 1. With only heights on the stack you can't recover the left boundary's index, so you can't compute width at all.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
stack.push(heights[i]);   // height only
// ... no way to know where this bar started
commonMistakesDetailed.good: stack.push(i);            // index — heights[i] is still reachable

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the flush sentinel
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Bars that never meet a shorter bar on their right stay on the stack forever. Without a final height-0 pass, their rectangles — often the largest — are never measured.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(n):        # stops at the last real bar
    ...
    stack.append(i)
return best                # leftover bars never popped
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(n + 1):    # one extra virtual bar
    h = 0 if i == n else heights[i]
    ...                    # flushes everything

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Width math after an empty pop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When the stack becomes empty after popping, the bar extends to the far left, so its width is i (positions 0..i-1), not i - 1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int width = i - stack.peek() - 1;  // crashes / wrong when empty
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int width = stack.isEmpty() ? i : i - stack.peek() - 1;
